actors.name: Haqqani Network (HQN)
actors.summary: Afghan-Pakistan militant network that joined the Taliban in the 1990s and remains deeply interwoven with Taliban senior leadership. The United States continues to designate HQN as a Foreign Terrorist Organization; Sirajuddin Haqqani is both a senior Taliban figure and the de facto Minister of Interior.

relationships.kind: closest ally relationship reported by UN

actors.name: ISIS-Khorasan (ISIS-K / ISKP)
actors.summary: Islamic State affiliate centered in Afghanistan and active across the Afghanistan-Pakistan-Central Asia theater. It remains the Taliban security apparatus's principal jihadist armed adversary and has maintained external-attack ambitions.

actors.name: Al-Qaida — Afghanistan Network
actors.summary: Al-Qaida elements remain present in Afghanistan according to UN monitoring, which reports that the Taliban maintains tight control over the group while continuing to host and support it. Senior commanders have been reported in Kabul, with relationships extending into Taliban and Haqqani networks.

actors.name: Al-Qaida in the Indian Subcontinent (AQIS)
actors.summary: Regional al-Qaida affiliate reported by the UN as active in southeastern Afghanistan. UN monitoring identifies the Haqqani Network as influential in the same area and reports continued AQIS activity.

relationships.kind: operates in areas of strong Haqqani influence

actors.name: Tehrik-e Taliban Pakistan (TTP)
actors.summary: Pakistan-focused militant umbrella with a major presence in Afghanistan. The 2025 UN Monitoring Team assessed roughly 6,000 fighters in Afghanistan across more than a dozen subgroups or factions and reported locations in Khost, Kunar, Nangarhar, Paktika and Paktiya.

relationships.kind: logistical/operational space relationship reported by UN

actors.name: Afghan Narcotics & Trafficking Networks
actors.summary: Distributed criminal networks involved in narcotics, precursor chemicals, smuggling and illicit finance. Cultivation and trafficking patterns have changed sharply under Taliban counternarcotics policies, but UNODC and Afghan law-enforcement reporting continue to document trafficking and synthetic-drug activity.
